w: Built as the Newport Casino, this complex of 13 grass courts plus hard, clay and indoor courts hosted the US National Championships (now the US Open) from 1881. It is a non-profit devoted to preserving and celebrating tennis, and since 1976 has run the Hall of Fame Open each July.
s: Where the US National Championships began in 1881
_facts: Former Newport Casino site
Hosted the US National Championships from 1881, precursor to the US Open
13 grass courts plus indoor, hard and clay courts
Hall of Fame Open held each July since 1976

w: Built 1898-1902 for silver heiress Theresa Fair Oelrichs, one of Newport's three great Gilded Age hostesses alongside Mrs Fish and Mrs Belmont of nearby Belcourt. Architect Stanford White modeled it on Versailles' Grand Trianon, adding a balustraded roofline that hides twenty servants' rooms and a laundry press room.
s: A Gilded Age mansion modeled on Versailles
_facts: Built 1898-1902 for Theresa Fair Oelrichs
Architect Stanford White modeled it on the Grand Trianon of Versailles
Also known as the Hermann Oelrichs House or J. Edgar Monroe House
Third storey hid 20 servants' rooms behind a balustraded roofline

w: Designed by Richard Morris Hunt for Oliver Hazard Perry Belmont and built 1891-94, Belcourt was meant for just six to eight weeks' use a year. Its European hodgepodge of French, Gothic, German, English and Italian decor folded extensive stables and carriage areas straight into the main house.
s: A 'cottage' used just six weeks a year
_facts: Built 1891-1894 by Richard Morris Hunt for Oliver Hazard Perry Belmont
On Bellevue Avenue, Newport
Mixes French Renaissance, Gothic, German, English and Italian styles
Stables and carriage areas built into the main structure

w: Built in 1763, this is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States, declared a National Historic Site in 1946. Its first congregants were Sephardic Jews who had migrated via West Indies trade routes; amid 18th-century upheaval they sent the deed and Torah scrolls to New York for safekeeping.
s: The oldest synagogue building standing in America
_facts: Built 1763, oldest surviving US synagogue building
Declared a National Historic Site in 1946
First congregants were Sephardic Jews from West Indies trade networks
Deed and Torah scrolls sent to New York for safekeeping amid 18th-century unrest

w: Ogden Goelet spent $4.5 million building this chateauesque mansion in 1892, making it Newport's second-largest cottage after The Breakers. Like Belcourt and Marble House, it was designed by Richard Morris Hunt, who gave Bellevue Avenue three of its grandest facades. It now anchors Salve Regina University's campus.
_facts: Built 1892 for Ogden Goelet at a cost of $4.5 million
Second-largest Newport mansion after The Breakers
Designed by Richard Morris Hunt, also architect of Belcourt and Marble House
Now owned by Salve Regina University

w: This red sandstone and granite manor, built 1887-92 for Frederick William Vanderbilt, borders the Cliff Walk with gardens originally laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted's firm. Tobacco heiress Doris Duke was its last private owner; her Newport Restoration Foundation now runs it as a museum, furnished much as she left it.
s: Doris Duke's manor on the Cliff Walk
_facts: English Manorial style, built 1887-1892 by Peabody & Stearns for Frederick William Vanderbilt
Gardens originally designed by Frederick Law Olmsted's firm
Borders the Cliff Walk, overlooking the Atlantic
Last owner Doris Duke; now run by the Newport Restoration Foundation

w: Designed by Richard Upjohn and built in 1839, this Gothic Revival cottage was among the first of Newport's summer 'cottages', predating the Gilded Age mansion boom by decades. Stanford White later extended it; the King family owned it from 1864 until giving it to the Preservation Society in 1972.
s: One of Newport's first summer cottages, 1839
_facts: Built 1839, designed by Richard Upjohn
Gothic Revival style, a National Historic Landmark
Later extended by George Champlin Mason and Stanford White
Owned by the King family 1864-1972, then given to the Preservation Society

w: Standing at the end of historic Ocean Drive, this lighthouse guides ships into Narragansett Bay's East Passage between Conanicut and Aquidneck Islands. It has become an unofficial symbol of Newport, a favorite backdrop for wedding photos, even though the surrounding land belongs to the Castle Hill Inn.
_facts: Located at the end of Ocean Drive
Active navigation aid for Narragansett Bay's East Passage
Popular site for weddings and marriage proposals
Owned by the US Coast Guard; land owned by Castle Hill Inn

w: Eighty-nine acres at Aquidneck Island's southwestern tip open onto wide views where Narragansett Bay meets the Atlantic. Part of Newport's Ocean Drive Historic District, the park sits beside Newport Country Club and is overseen by staff based at neighboring Fort Adams State Park.
s: Wide Atlantic views along Ocean Drive
_facts: 89 acres at the southwestern tip of Aquidneck Island
Part of the Ocean Drive Historic District
Adjacent to Newport Country Club
Managed alongside Fort Adams State Park

w: Officially the Church of the Holy Name of Mary, this is the oldest Catholic parish in Rhode Island. Its lasting fame, though, comes from one wedding: in 1953 it hosted the marriage of Jacqueline Bouvier to Senator, and future president, John F. Kennedy.
s: Where Jackie Bouvier married JFK in 1953
_facts: Oldest Catholic parish church in Rhode Island
At 14 William Street, corner of Spring Street
Site of Jacqueline Bouvier and JFK's 1953 wedding
Part of the Diocese of Providence

w: Established July 4, 1799 and named for John Adams, this coastal fort's current stone bulk was built 1824-57 under the Third System of US defenses. Its first commander, Captain John Henry, later helped trigger the War of 1812. Today the fort anchors Fort Adams State Park on Newport Harbor.
_facts: Established July 4, 1799, named for John Adams
Current fort built 1824-1857 as a Third System coastal fortification
First commander Captain John Henry, later tied to the War of 1812
Now part of Fort Adams State Park

w: New York architect Charles A. Platt designed this French chateau-style house in 1927 for banker William Fahnestock, making it one of the last great mansions built in Newport before the era of such construction ended. It stands within the Ochre Point-Cliffs Historic District.
s: One of the last great Newport mansions, 1927
_facts: Built 1927, designed by Charles A. Platt
Built for New York banker William Fahnestock
French chateau style
Part of the Ochre Point-Cliffs Historic District

w: In 1780, General Rochambeau's 6,000-strong French army landed here to reinforce the American Revolution, an event marked since 1928 by a Newport Historical Society monument. The park's stone pier once launched America's Cup regattas, until hurricanes destroyed the wooden finger docks, which were never rebuilt.
_facts: Site of Rochambeau's 6,000-troop French landing in 1780
Rochambeau monument erected by the Newport Historical Society in 1928
Land donated by the Edward King heirs in 1897
Stone pier once served America's Cup regattas
